CORE PRINCIPLES

The Three Ways

1

Flow

Work moves left to right, fast, in small batches, with nothing piling up in between.

2

Feedback

Problems travel right to left, fast, so they're fixed at the source instead of downstream.

3

Continual learning

Improving the system is part of the work: experiment, learn from failure, share it.

Kim, Humble, Debois, Willis: The DevOps Handbook

FIRST WAY · FLOW

Work in progress sets your lead time

LITTLE'S LAW

lead time =
WIP ÷ throughput

Start more work without finishing faster, and everything takes longer.

  • Limit work in progress
  • Shrink the batch size
  • Make the queues visible
  • Stop starting, start finishing

FIRST WAY · THE CONSTRAINT

Every system has one bottleneck

An hour saved at the bottleneck is an hour saved for the whole system. An hour saved anywhere else is an illusion.

Identify

Exploit

Subordinate

Elevate

Repeat: it moves

After Eliyahu Goldratt, The Goal (1984)

SECOND WAY · FEEDBACK

Find problems while they're cheap

Fast CI

A slow suite makes every failure cost more, because the code keeps moving while you wait.

Stop the line

When defects show up, fix the source before shipping more of them.

Telemetry

Most of the time to restore service is the time to notice it's broken.

THIRD WAY · CONTINUAL LEARNING

Improving the work is the work

Kaizen time

Reserve capacity to improve the system, not just run it. Skipping it compounds.

Blameless reviews

Blame is faster today, and it hides tomorrow's incidents from you.

Experiment

Small, safe-to-fail changes teach faster than big bets.

MEASURING IT

The four DORA keys

THROUGHPUT

Lead time for changes

Deployment frequency

STABILITY

Change failure rate

Time to restore service

The finding that matters: speed and stability move together. The best teams don't trade one for the other.

Forsgren, Humble, Kim: Accelerate (2018) · dora.dev

THE QUESTION FOR TODAY

What happens to all of this when writing code becomes nearly free?

THE DEBRIEF

What the game was showing you

1

Less in flight, more shipped

Opening the limits felt productive. It made more work go stale, and less of it shipped.

2

The bottleneck moved to Review

Adding people or agents anywhere else changed nothing, or made it worse.

3

Agents paid off only once review could keep up

Idle agents meant a review problem, not a capacity one. A person moved to Review is what let them work.

THE ANSWER THE GAME GIVES

Human attention is the constraint.

Agents add doing. Only people add judgment. And money can't buy more attention.

THE LAST YEAR

Four changes since agents joined the loop

1 · Planning is a bottleneck

Agents amplify a vague spec. Intent has to be written down before anyone, or anything, starts.

2 · Review is the constraint

Producing a change got cheap. Reading one carefully didn't.

3 · WIP explodes

Ten parallel agent branches is one click. Drift and conflicts grow faster than the branch count.

4 · Agent review rubber-stamps

It catches mechanical defects and misses design ones. The dashboard looks great.

THE RESEARCH

Output went up. Delivery mostly didn't.

+98% PRs · +91% review

Faros AI, 10,000+ developers: high-AI teams merged twice the PRs and waited far longer for review. No org-level DORA gain.

1.7× issues per PR

CodeRabbit, 470 open-source PRs: AI-authored changes carried more issues, logic and correctness errors most of all.

19% slower, felt faster

METR trial, early-2025 tools: experienced developers were slower with AI but believed they'd been 20% faster.

AI is an amplifier

DORA 2025, ~5,000 professionals: AI magnifies a team's existing strengths and its existing weaknesses.

Faros AI (2025) · CodeRabbit (Dec 2025) · METR (Jul 2025) · DORA State of AI-assisted Software Development (2025)

CASE · JULY 2025 · REPLIT AND SAASTR

An instruction is not a control

  • SaaStr's founder built an app with Replit's agent over twelve days, in plain English.
  • During an explicit code freeze, the agent ran destructive commands and wiped the production database: about 1,200 executives and 1,200 companies.
  • It then said a rollback was impossible. It wasn't.

WHAT CHANGED

Replit separated development and production databases and added a planning-only mode.

The Register, 21–22 Jul 2025 · Fortune, 23 Jul 2025 · AI Incident Database #1152

CASE · DECEMBER 2025 · AWS

"Delete and recreate"

  • Engineers let Kiro, Amazon's agentic coding tool, fix an issue in a production environment.
  • It decided the fix was to delete and recreate the environment. Reported result: a 13-hour Cost Explorer outage in one region.
  • Two-person approval existed. The agent inherited an engineer's broader permissions and went around it.

WHAT CHANGED

Amazon called it user error in access controls, and added mandatory peer review for production changes.

Financial Times, Feb 2026, via AI Incident Database #1442 · Amazon statement, 21 Feb 2026

CASE · MARCH 2026 · AMAZON RETAIL

A code safety reset

  • A run of retail site outages in early March was linked, in internal documents, to AI-assisted code changes.
  • The response: a 90-day code safety reset for critical systems.
  • And senior engineers must now sign off on AI-assisted changes from junior and mid-level engineers.

THE PATTERN

At one of the most automated companies there is, the answer to agent-scale change was more senior attention, spent at review.

TechRadar and Fortune, March 2026, reporting an internal Amazon email

CASE · 2025 · HUMANLAYER

"Nobody read the code"

  • Dex Horthy's team stopped reading agent-written code. Agents handled tickets, crashes and code review.
  • About three months in, production broke. No amount of prompting got Opus 4.1 to find the root cause.
  • Days of digging by hand found a primary key routed through the whole codebase that needed its own table. Then three weeks re-onboarding to code no one had read.

WHAT CHANGED

"None of these things have intuition for software architecture." He no longer thinks skipping review pays off, now that agents write 10x to 100x more code.

Dex Horthy, "Context engineering with Dex Horthy", The Pragmatic Engineer, 15 Jul 2026, 44:01 to 45:39

PLANNING

[What you now require before an agent starts work]

[A change an agent got confidently wrong, and who caught it]

WHERE THE ATTENTION GOES

Humans at both ends, agents in the middle

HUMAN

Plan

Intent, acceptance criteria, and what not to touch, written down

AGENTS

Build

Cheap, fast, parallel, and held to a WIP limit

HUMAN

Review

Read it with AI help, understand it, own the merge

Every case we just looked at ended by adding attention at one of these two ends.

AGENT REVIEW

Agents check the code. People check the decision.

MECHANICAL FIXES

Let agent review clear them

  • Bugs and missed edge cases
  • Error handling, style, tests
  • Everything needed is in the diff

DESIGN DECISIONS

Keep a person on them

  • Is this the right change at all?
  • The right abstraction, the right reading of the ask
  • How it fits the other work in flight

An agent's approval says the code is correct. It can't say the change is right, because the intent isn't in the diff.

FOR MONDAY

Three things to take back

1

Budget attention like capacity

Cap agent work in flight at what your reviewers can actually read. Count review hours, not agent seats.

2

Put people at plan and review

Written intent before work starts, and a person who owns every merge. No agent-only path to production.

3

Measure true quality

Track change failure rate, rework and escaped defects. PR counts and approvals are too easy to satisfy.

Code is cheap. Attention isn't. Spend it where the constraint is.
